newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD commends Irish, Dutch fight on unemployment.
newsitem.headline: OECD commends Irish, Dutch fight on unemployment.

text.p: Unemployment in OECD countries has risen in the 1990s and the number of member countries which have seen a rise in structural unemployment far outweighs those who have managed to reduce it, a report released on Monday shows.

The report, which was produced to coincide with the OECD's annual ministerial meeting on Monday and Tuesday, said Ireland and the Netherlands had joined the ranks of those successfully attacking structural unemployment in line with OECD advice.

It highlights wage moderation and the reduction of payroll taxes as the main reasons for a fall in structural unemployment in the Netherlands and attributes Ireland's progress to cutting unemployment benefit and improved education.
Structural unemployment in Ireland fell to 12.8 percent in 1996 from 16.0 percent in 1990, while it fell to 6.3 from 7.0 percent in the Netherlands.

The Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development produced a "Jobs Study" in 1994 which advised member countries to tackle joblessness by reforming unemployment benefit and tax, increasing work-time, wage and labour cost flexibility as well as improving education and training and removing disincentives to enterprise.

The latest report, designed to follow up on progress since then and encourage member countries to follow the more liberal approach espoused by the OECD through peer pressure, says the results have been mixed so far.

"Over the 1990s, unemployment in the OECD area as a whole rose from the already unacceptably high level at the end of the previous decade," says the report. "Most of this increase was cyclical, but structural unemployment may also have gone up."

The report says the trend in structural unemployment, which strips out the proportion of joblessness attributed to ups and downs of economic cycles, varies from country to country -- in part according to the extent to which governments see a need to reconcile labour market policy and social stability and equity.

Overall unemployment among 23 of the 29 member countries -- the most recent members are not included -- rose to 7.7 percent in 1996 from 6.1 percent in 1990 and stood at the same 7.7 percent level a decade earlier, in 1986, the report says.
Structural unemployment stood at 7.1 percent in 1996, versus 6.8 percent at the start of the decade and 7.0 percent in 1986.
"Among individual countries, already high structural unemployment appears to have risen further over the 1990s in Spain, Italy and to a minor extent in France," it says.

"In Finland and Sweden, structural unemployment has risen abruptly from already low levels," it says, adding that there have also been rises in a number of small European countries with traditionally low unemployment levels.
The report, like others in the past, finds little fault with policy in the United States, Britain or New Zealand, where a markedly more free-market approach has long been embraced.
"The big non-European member countries, including the United States, Japan and Canada, have broadly stable structural unemployment rates, as have some European countries," it says.

"The most encouraging developments were registered in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Netherlands and New Zealand, where falls in structural unemployment rates either began or continued in the course of the 1990s."

Among the big European states where structural unemployment has risen -- from 6.9 percent in 1990 to 9.6 percent in 1996 in Germany and from 9.3 to 9.7 percent in France in the same period -- the OECD recommends shortening the duration of unemployment benefit and says unemployment benefit in Germany should be used to "encourage lower-paid employment".

It also proposes tightening up on early retirement schemes in both countries, reducing labour, income and other payroll taxes in Germany and for France suggests cutting payroll tax in low-wage sectors.
